title: How to Protect Yourself From Ticks
hook: Tick season is here, and a single bite can pass on Lyme and other diseases. A few simple habits sharply cut the risk.
key_points: Use an EPA-registered repellent (like DEET or picaridin) on skin, and treat clothing and gear with permethrin.
Stick to the center of trails — ticks wait in tall grass, brush, and leaf litter.
Do a full-body tick check after being outdoors: scalp, behind the knees, and the waistline.
Remove an attached tick promptly with fine tweezers, pulling straight up — the sooner it's off, the lower the risk.
Watch for an expanding rash or fever in the days after a bite, and see a doctor if they appear.
content_html: Warm months bring people outdoors — and ticks, tiny arachnids that can transmit Lyme disease and several other illnesses through a single bite. NPR asked two experts how to stay safe.
extra_html:
Prevention starts before you head out. Apply an EPA-registered insect repellent such as DEET or picaridin to exposed skin, and treat clothing, shoes, and gear with permethrin. Outdoors, stick to the center of trails and steer clear of tall grass, brush, and leaf litter, where ticks wait to latch on.

Afterward, do a careful full-body check — including the scalp, behind the knees, and around the waistline — and check kids and pets too; showering soon after coming inside helps. If you find a tick attached, remove it promptly with fine-tipped tweezers, grasping close to the skin and pulling straight up. Because most tick-borne diseases take hours of attachment to transmit, fast removal is one of the best protections you have. In the days that follow, watch for an expanding rash or flu-like symptoms, and see a doctor if they show up.

related.title: When a Symptom Needs a Doctor
related.hook: Most everyday symptoms pass on their own. The skill worth having is recognizing the red flags that mean don't wait — call for help now.

related.title: This Tick Can Give You a Meat Allergy
related.hook: The lone star tick is spreading across much of the U.S. — and its bite can trigger alpha-gal syndrome, a delayed allergic reaction to red meat.

flashcards.prompt: What's the most important habit after spending time outdoors in tick season?
flashcards.back_html: Do a full-body tick check — scalp, behind the knees, the waistline — and remove any attached tick promptly with fine tweezers. The sooner it's off, the lower the disease risk.

flashcards.prompt: What's the right way to remove an attached tick?

choices.text: Grasp it with fine tweezers and pull straight up
Burn it off with a lit match
Smother it in petroleum jelly and wait

flashcards.explanation_html: Steady, straight-up pressure with fine tweezers removes the whole tick cleanly. Burning or smothering it is slower and can make things worse — prompt removal is what matters.

flashcards.prompt: Which of these actually helps prevent tick bites?

choices.text: Wearing dark clothing so ticks can't be seen
Walking through tall grass and brush

flashcards.explanation_html: Repellent and permethrin-treated clothing keep ticks off. Light-colored clothing helps you spot them, and tall grass and brush are exactly where ticks wait — so avoid them.
